paras: The lynching of four rustlers near Mesilla was the killing, in New Mexico Territory in June 1882, of four unnamed men accused of robbing a store, who were overtaken by a posse and strangled. A Las Vegas dispatch described the dead as Americans from a gang of Arizona cowboys and the posse as Mexican, and said the men "richly deserved their fate." The story spread through the national telegraph columns within days but is known only from that single dispatch.

According to the dispatch, four "rustlers" had recently bound and gagged Mason, a storekeeper near Mesilla, and robbed his store "of all they could carry." The men were said to belong to "a gang of Arizona cowboys," and their names were not known.

A posse pursued the four and, once it had overtaken them, strangled all of them. The dispatch gave no place, date or hour for the killing and no number for the posse, which it called "a Mexican posse"; a Montana brief called it "a party of Mexicans." Shorter versions said the men were "hung" or "hanged" rather than strangled.

No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage, and no New Mexico or Arizona paper's account was found. At year's end a Michigan chronology listed the case under June 13 as "Four murderers lynched at Mesilla, N. M.," calling the dead murderers rather than robbers.

The special, dated Las Vegas, June 14, reached western dailies the next morning, often by way of Chicago. Headlines varied in emphasis: the Sacramento Record-Union ran "Four Cowboys Lynched by Mexicans," the Los Angeles Herald "Four Rustlers Strangled," and the Seattle Post-Intelligencer "Justice, If not Law." Most papers kept the closing judgment that the men "richly deserved their fate," though the St. Landry Democrat in Louisiana dropped it in July.

Weeklies in Wisconsin, Dakota, Michigan, Minnesota, Illinois and Kansas reran the dispatch or a one-line condensation in crime columns during late June. The Hand County Press set it beside lynchings of Black men in Kansas, Kentucky and South Carolina and a remark that lynching was "becoming a common occurrence." The Ottawa Free Trader printed it under "Judge Lynch" and the Barbour County Index under "LYNCHED."

The Indiana State Sentinel's version read "All were Mexicans" where every other printing of the same dispatch read "All were Americans," which suggests a copying error. Accounts of the date and place also differed: a Montana brief put the hanging near Mesilla "on the 14th inst.," while the Ottawa Free Trader placed it "At Las Vegas, New Mexico, on the 13th," apparently mistaking the dispatch's dateline for the scene.

bases: The dispatch says four men accused of robbing a store were pursued, 'overtaken by a Mexican posse and strangled', and several papers headed it a lynching (A1, A2, A15).

Four men accused of robbery were killed without trial by a pursuing 'posse' or 'party of Mexicans' that the papers headed as a lynching, and the dispatch said they 'richly deserved their fate' (A1, A2, A8). The victims are described as 'Americans' and Arizona cowboys, and no paper suggests they were Black (A1, A10).
Every report traces to one Las Vegas, N. M., special of June 14, reprinted or condensed nationally; no local, eyewitness or follow-up account was found (A1, A2, A9).
